category_title: Independent learners who struggle to visualize spatial relationships in three-dimensional word problems
minimal_context: The student is working on a multistep word problem about fitting a long pole in the back of a loading truck using a provided 2D diagram of a rectangular prism.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's look at this next multistep word problem about fitting a long pole in the back of a loading truck. Here is the diagram of the rectangular prism with the labeled dimensions.

STUDENT: Is it still Pythagorean Theorem? I’m not sure yet, because we don’t know the whole truck.

TUTOR: How would you start setting it up on your scratch paper?

STUDENT: Y eah, by drawing a picture of it like out of the truck. (She drew a triangle using dimensions given, but not the right dimensions.) It’s 5 and 4 as the legs?

TUTOR: Take another look at the dimensions you chose for that triangle.

STUDENT: Oh man. Y eah, is that supposed to be the way it is farthest in the truck? (Starts to guess again using a different combination of dimensions.) Is the next one going to be in here?

options.A: Constantly probe the student with questions to check for their understanding of the rectangular prism diagram during the activity.
options.B: Draw some diagonals on the diagram, label more of the dimensions, and provide explicit explanations of the mathematical relationships within the problem.
options.C: Choose exploratory geometry activities that are neither too challenging nor too easy for the student during the session.
options.D: Provide the student with opportunities to respond to math questions at a pace that maximizes learning and engagement.
